crassus, a, um, adj.
Sanscr. kart-, to spin; cf.: crates, cartilago, etc.
; as opp. to flowing, thin, lean, delicate, etc.,
solid, thick, dense, fat, gross, etc. (freq. and class. in prose and poetry).
Lit.: semina (opp. liquida),; cf.: crassius semen,: corpus,: unguentum,: paludes,: cruor,: aquae,greatly swollen,: ager,; ; cf.: terga (agri),: homo,: turdi,: toga,; cf. filum,; : restis,: digiti crassi tres, as a measure,.—
Esp., of the atmosphere, thick, dense, heavy: aër crassus et concretus,; cf.: crassissimus aër,: caelum Thebis (opp. tenue Athenis),: Baeotum in crasso jurares aëre natum,; : caligo nubis, Lucr.

6, 461; cf.: caliginis aër Crassior,: vitrum crassiore visu,less transparent,.—

Trop. (rare; not in Cic.): crassum infortunium,i. e. a sound beating,: senes, stupid, dull, Varr. ap. : Ofellus Rusticus abnormis sapiens crassāque Minervā,i. e. dull, stolid,; cf.: crassiore ut vocant Musa,: turba,uncultivated,: neglegentia,stupid, clumsy,: crassiora nomina, more rude or barbarous, ; cf. .—Hence, adv.: crassē (rare; not in Cic.), thickly.
Lit.: picare vasa,; cf. oblinere,.—
Grossly, rudely: crasse illepideve compositum poëma (the figure taken from a coarse web),.—Of precious stones, not clearly, dimly (comp.), ; .—Hence of the indistinct understanding of any thing, not clearly, confusedly: crasse et summatim et obscure intellegere aliquid,.

la:verb:credo.gloss: to believe, to trust in, to give credence to
senses: to believe, to trust in, to give credence to
to confide in, have confidence in
to commit or consign something to one for preservation, protection, etc., to entrust to one
la:verb:credo.html:
crēdo, dĭdi, dĭtum, 3 (
pres. subj. creduam, : creduas,; : creduat,; : creduis,; : creduit,; inf. credier, ; crevi for credidi,), v. a.
Sanscr. crat, crad, trust, and dha-; v. 2. do
.
Orig. belonging to the lang. of business, to give as a loan, to loan, lend, make or loan to any one: (vilicus) injussu domini credat nemini; quod dominus crediderit, exigat,: quibus credas male,; cf. populis,: alicui grandem pecuniam,; so, pecunias ei,; and: pecuniae creditae,: centum talenta,: solutio rerum creditarum, et saep.—Hence,
crēdĭtum, i, n., a loan, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.—
Transf. beyond the circle of business (very freq. in every period and species of composition).
With the prevailing idea of intended protection, to commit or consign something to one for preservation, protection, etc., to intrust to one, = committo, commendo (cf. concredo): ubi is obiit mortem, qui mihi id aurum credidit, (credere est servandum commendare, ); so, nummum, (for which , concredere): alicujus fidei potestatique (with committere),; cf. , § 14: vitam ac fortunas meas, Lucil. ap. ; cf. : militi arma,: se suaque omnia alienissimis,: se ponto,: se perfidis hostibus,: se ventis,: pennis se caelo,; cf. : se pugnae, et saep.: crede audacter quid lubet,: facinus magnum timido pectori,: illi consilia omnia,: arcanos sensus tibi,; cf.: arcana libris,: aliquid cerae,.—Poet., with in and acc.: inque novos soles audent se germina tuto Credere,.—
With the prevailing idea of bestowing confidence, to trust to or confide in a person or thing, to have confidence in, to trust.
With dat.: virtuti suorum satis credere,; cf. : praesenti fortunae,: consules magis non confidere quam non credere suis militibus,rather mistrusted their intentions than their valor,: nec jam amplius hastae,: ne nimium colori,: bibulis talaribus,.—Freq. in eccl. Lat.: Moysi et mihi,: verbis meis,.—
Esp., with in and acc. of pers., to believe in, trust in (eccl. Lat.): hoc est ergo credere in Deum, credendo adhaerere ad bene coöperandum bona operanti Deo,: qui fidem habet sine spe ac dilectione, Christum esse credit, non in Christum credit,: qui credit in Filium habet vitam aeternam, et saep.—
To trust one in his declarations, assertions, etc., i. e. to give him credence, to believe: injurato, scio, plus credet mihi, quam jurato tibi,: vin' me istuc tibi, etsi incredibile'st, credere?: credit jam tibi de isto,: cui omnium rerum ipsus semper credit,in every thing,; cf. : diu deliberandum et concoquendum est, utrum potius Chaereae injurato in suā lite, an Manilio et Luscio juratis in alieno judicio credatis,.—
Mihi crede, believe me, confide in my words, upon my word, ἐμοὶ πιθοῦ, an expression of confirmation, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.; ; ; cf.: mihi credite, 2, 7, 15; ; ; —In the same sense (but more rare in Cic.): crede mihi,; ; ; ; Sulp. ap. ; ; ; : crede igitur mihi,: credite mihi,.—
Credor in poets several times equivalent to creditur mihi: certe credemur, ait, si verba sequatur Exitus,; so : creditus accepit cantatas protinus herbas, etc.,; so in part., ; cf.: (Cassandra) non umquam credita Teucris,.—
Sibi, to believe one's self, trust one's own convictions, be fully convinced: cum multa dicta sunt sapienter et graviter, tum vel in primis, crede nobis, crede tibi,: fieri malunt alieni erroris accessio, quam sibi credere,: non satis sibi ipsi credebant, Auct. B. Alex. 6:—
With simple reference to the object mentioned or asserted, to believe a thing, hold or admit as true: velim te id quod verum est credere, Lucil. ap. ; cf.: credo et verum est, Afer ap. : me miseram! quid jam credas? aut cur credas?: quod fere libenter homines id quod volunt credunt,; cf. : audivi ista ... sed numquam sum addictus ut crederem,: ne quid de se temere crederent,: res Difficilis ad credundum,; cf. et saep.—Pass.: res tam scelesta ... credi non potest,.—Pass. impers.: in quo scelere, etiam cum multae causae convenisse unum in locum atque inter se congruere videntur, tamen non temere creditur,.—
In gen. = opinor, arbitror, to be of opinion, to think, believe, suppose.
With acc.: timeo ne aliud credam atque aliud nunties,: quae deserta et inhospita tesqua credis,: fortem crede bonumque,: quos gravissimos sapientiae magistros aetas vetus credidit,.—Pass.: potest ... falsum aliquid pro vero credi,: origo animi caelestis creditur,; , prooem. § 24: Evander venerabilior divinitate creditā Carmentae matris,.—
With acc. and inf. (so most freq.): jam ego vos novisse credo, ut sit pater meus,: cum reliquum exercitum subsequi crederet,: caelo tonantem credidimus Jovem Regnare. et saep.: victos crederes,one would have thought, one might have imagined,; so ; cf. Zumpt, Lat. Gr. § 528.—Pass.: navis praeter creditur ire,: quem (Athin) peperisse Limnate creditur,: creditus est optime dixisse,; cf. —Impers.: credetur abesse ab eo culpam,: neque sine causā creditum est, stilum non minus agere cum delet,— So in the abl. part. pass. credito, with acc. and inf., ; .—
Absol.: credo inserted, like opinor, puto, etc., and the Gr. οἶμαι, as a considerate, polite, or ironical expression of one's opinion, I believe, as I think, I suppose, I dare say, etc.: credo, misericors est,; so placed first,; ; ; ; ; ; ; : Mulciber, credo, arma fecit,; so ; ; ; ; et saep.: aut jam hic aderit, credo hercle, aut jam adest,.

la:adj:creber.html:
crēber, bra, brum (
sup. creberrimus; but crebrissimus,; cf. Rudd. I. p. 170; and CEREBERRIMVS,), adj.
from cre-, root of cresco, Corn. Beitr. p. 356
, that exists or takes place in a continuous multitude, following closely together or one after another (hence with continuus, ; opp. rarus).
Thick, close, pressed together, frequent, numerous, repeated (very freq., and class.).
Of material subjects: lucus avius, Crebro salicto oppletus,; cf. silva,: crebris arboribus succisis omnes introitus erant praeclusi,: rami,: (venae et arteriae) crebrae multaeque, toto corpore intextae,: funale,numerous torches,: castella,: creberrima aedificia,: ignes quam creberrimi,; cf. : vigilias ponere,: tanto crebriores litterae nuntiique,; cf. exploratores,: tam crebri ad terram decidebant quam pira,as thick as pears,; cf. hostes,: crebri cecidere caelo lapides,; cf. sup., et saep.—
Of immaterial subjects: itiones,; cf. excursiones,: ictus,; ; : impetus,; : anhelitus,; : commutationes aestuum,: rumores,: amplexus,: compellationes,: sonus,oft repeated,: argumentatio,: supplosio pedis,: crebriores figurae,: quae apud Sallustium rare fuerunt, apud hunc crebra sunt et paene continua,: crebra lumina (dicendi) et continua,.—
Meton., of an object that is furnished with abundance, or produces something in multitudes, crowded with, abundant, abounding in: creber harundinibus lucus,: Africus procellis,: Tiberis creber ac subitus incrementis,.—Esp., of speech or writing: sane in eo creber fuisti, Te noluisse, etc.,you frequently said,: si mihi tantum esset otii, quantum est tibi ... in scribendo multo essem crebrior quam tu,: (Thucydides) ita creber est rerum frequentia, ut, etc.,; : quis sententiis aut acutior aut crebrior? id. ap. ; (cf.: densus sententiis, id.

ib. § 68).—In Gr. constr., of the person: densis ictibus heros Creber utrāque manu pulsat versatque Dareta,: modus (dicendi) translationibus crebrior,.—Hence, advv.,

Most freq. in the form crēbrō, close one after another (in time or number), repeatedly, often, oftentimes, frequently, many times: si crebro cades,: ruri esse,: mittere litteras,: tussire et exspuere,: personare purgatam aurem, et saep.: qui crebro Catulum, saepe me, saepissime rem publicam nominabat,.—Comp. crebrius: perlucet villa crebrius quam cribrum,i. e. with more holes, openings,: mittas litteras,: crebrius aut perfidiosius rebellantes,.— Sup. creberrime (creberru-): commemorantur a Stoicis,.—
crē-bră (acc. plur.; cf. Rudd. II. p. 159), repeatedly: revisit ad stabulum (mater),: et pede terram Crebra ferit (equus),.—
crēbrē, closely, compactly (of place; only in Vitr.): fundamenta aedificiorum palationibus crebre fixa,.—Sup.: crates ex virgis creberrime textae,.—*
crē-brĭter, repeatedly, frequently (in time), ; cf. Hand, Turs. II. p. 133 sq.

la:noun:crux.gloss: wooden frame on which criminals were crucified, especially a cross
senses: wooden frame on which criminals were crucified, especially a cross
gallows bird; one who deserves to be hanged
la:noun:crux.html:
crux, ŭcis, f. (m., Enn. ap. ; Gracch. ap. Fest. s. v. masculino, p. 150, 24, and 151, 12 Müll.) [perh. kindred with circus].
Lit.
In gen., a tree, frame, or other wooden instruments of execution, on which criminals were impaled or hanged, ; sqq.—
In partic., a cross, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ,

47; et saep.: dignus fuit qui malo cruce periret, Gracch. ap. Fest. l. l.: pendula,the pole of a carriage,. —

Transf.
As a term of reproach, a gallows bird, a hempen rascal, .—
Transf., torture, trouble, misery, destruction, etc. (so most freq. in Plaut. and Ter., and in the former esp. freq. in connection with mala): aliqua mala crux, tormentor (of a prostitute), ; cf.: illae cruces,: quae te mala crux agitat?what tormentor troubles you?: abstraxit hominem in maximam malam crucem,: quaerere in malo crucem,.—Prov.: summum jus antiqui summam putabant crucem,.—Hence, in colloq. lang.: I (abi, etc.) in malam crucem!go to the devil! go and be hanged!; ; ; ; cf.: Cy. Num quid vis? Me. Ut eas maximam in malam crucem, ; .—Without mala: I in crucem,.—And ellipt.: in malam crucem!; . —Hence, Ital. croce; Fr. croix.

la:adv:cras.html:
crās, adv.
root ka-, ku-, to lighten, burn; Gr. καίω; cf. Sanscr. cvas, the same
,
to-morrow, αὔριον (freq. and class.).
With tempp. fut.: rus cras cum filio Cum primo luci ibo hinc,: scies fortasse cras, summum perendie,: cras donaberis haedo,: Qui non est hodie, cras minus aptus erit, et saep.—With ellipsis of verb: negat Eros hodie: cras mane putat (sc. venturum esse),early to-morrow morning,.—
With temp. pres.: sat habeo, si cras fero,; : cras est mihi Judicium,; Atta ap. :. cras nato Caesare festus dat veniam somnumque dies, —As the title of a writing of Varro: Cras credo, hodie nihil, of which there are some fragments ap. —
Subst.: cras istud quando venit? sqq.; so, hesternum,.—*
= in diem crastinum, on or for the morrow: cras te non vocavi,.—

la:adj:crispus.html:
crispus, a, um, adj.
kindred with crinis, crista; cf. cresco
.
Originally of the hair, curled, crisped, crimped: cincinni,; cf. coma,; and: leo crispioribus jubis,.—Of persons, having curled hair, curlyheaded, ; ; .—*
Trop., of discourse, artistic, elaborate: crispum agmen orationis,; cf. crispulus, II.—
Transf.
Curled, uneven, waving, wrinkled: parietes abiete crispā, Enn. ap. . 44: brassica,: crispae frondis apium,: acer montanum crispius,: (marmor) Augusteum undatim crispum,: lactuca crispissimi folii, et saep.—
In tremulous motion, quivering, tremulous: linguae bisulcae jactu crispo fulgere, Pac. ap. ; : pecten (i. e. plectrum),: aër subtili nebulā,.

la:noun:crimen.gloss: a judicial decision, verdict, or judgment
senses: a judicial decision, verdict, or judgment
a cause of a crime; criminal
a charge, accusation, reproach; calumny, slander
the fault one is accused of; crime, misdeed, offence, fault
la:noun:crimen.html:
crīmen, ĭnis, n.
contr. for cernimen, from cerno, II. C.
; lit.,
a judicial decision, verdict, judgment; hence, transf., like the Gr. κρῖμα, of the subject of such a decision, and with partieular reference either to the accuser or to the accused.
Subject., or with reference to the accuser, a charge, accusation, reproach; esp. when unfounded, a calumny, slander (very freq. in every period and species of composition): criminin' me habuisse fidem?; cf. : hae litterae fidem Persei criminibus fecerunt,: cum respondero criminibus,: se falsis criminibus circumventum,; cf.: crimen falsum,; : criminibus adversariorum in invidiam venire,: sermones pleni criminum in Patres,: crimina et suspiciones,: tanti maleficii crimen probare te censes posse talibus viris, si, etc.,: sceleris maximi,; cf. ; : istius conjurationis,: avaritiae,; : veneficii,: ubi est crimen quod reprehenditis?i. e. the point of the accusation, Halm ad loc.: quo enim illi crimine peccatoque perierunt?: haec causa est omnium horum scelerum atque criminum,; so (approaching the signif. II. A. infra), id C. Norbano in nefario crimine atque in fraude capitali esse ponendum, Sorof ad loc.: era in crimen veniet, (era male audiet, Don.): quid? sciebas tibi crimini datum iri?would be made a reproach?; cf. : crimen adferre,; cf.: crimen inferre, offerre,: in quos crimen intendebatur,: esse in crimine,to stand charged with,: propulsare,: defendere,to repel, confute,; ; and opp. obicere,: repellere, transferre, et saep.—Poet.: belli, pretexts (causae), .—*
Meton. (abstr. pro concreto), an object of reproach or invective: perpetuae crimen posteritatis eris,.—
Object., or with reference to the accused, the fault complained of, a crime, fault, offence (freq., but rare in ante-Aug. prose).
Lit.
Ingen.: foedati crimine turpi,: cum haec (causa) non in crimine aliquo, quod ille posset infitiari ... consisteret, Sorof ad loc.: crimen meum indicare,; : carendum non solum crimine turpitudinis, verum etiam suspicione,: cum quidam crimen ultro faterentur,: velut crimen taedas exosa jugales,: non prodere vultu,: scire,: hoc si crimen erit, crimen amoris erit, cf.: tuum crimen erit,thy fault,: crimina et innoxios discernere,.—Ovid in his Tristia very freq. calls the offence on account of which he was banished crimina or crimen, interchanging it with error, e. g. 1, 9, 64; 2, 3; 2, 207; 3, 5, 52; 3, 6, 26 al.—
Of inanim. objects: crimina brassicae sunt, animae gravitatem facere, etc.,fault, defect,, § 91.—
In partic., the crime of lewdness, adultery, ; .—
Meton.
An object representing a crime: et rupit pictas, caelestia crimina, vestes, i. e. deorum adulteria,; cf.: tum paries nullo crimine pictus erat, (2, 5, 26 Bip.): impressā signat sua crimina gemmā,a letter containing her crime,.—
A cause of a crime, a criminal: se causam clamat crimenque caputque malorum,; cf.: a pereant Baiae, crimen amoris, aquae,: Crimen et illa fuit ... Myrrha, (4, 18), 15.

la:adj:crudelis.html:
crūdēlis, e, adj.
cf. Gr. κρύος; Lat. crudus, cruor, caro
,
morally rude or unfeeling, with exclusive reference to conduct towards persons or things, hard, unmerciful, hard-hearted, cruel, severe, fierce (freq. and class. in prose and poetry).
Of living subjects.
With in and abl.: crudeles gaudent in tristi funere fratris, ; cf.: crudelis in calamitate hominis consularis,: cui nimis videtur senatus in conservandā patriā fuisse crudelis,.—

crūdēlĕ (prop. neutr. sing. of adj.), cruelly, etc., ; ; . —
crūdēlĭter, cruelly, in a cruel manner (very freq.), ; ; ; ; ; —Comp., ; ; .—Sup., ; ; ; et saep.
